analysis.one_liner: Gives farmworkers the same overtime and minimum wage protections as other workers, phased in over seven years.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than being referred to the Senate labor committee: it never got a hearing or vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, backed by 15 Democratic and Independent senators and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: Farmworkers are the one large group of hourly workers still denied the basic federal labor protections most workers have had since 1938: many get no overtime until they pass 60 hours a week, some are exempt from minimum wage entirely, and children can legally work long hours on farms. This bill would delete those exemptions from the Fair Labor Standards Act, requiring time-and-a-half pay after 55 hours a week starting in 2024, stepping down to 40 hours by 2027 (2030 for farms with 25 or fewer employees). It never received a committee hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly two million farmworkers, a workforce that is heavily immigrant and Latino, would gain overtime pay after a 40-hour week (after a multi-year phase-in), minimum wage coverage for workers currently exempt, and the loss of exemptions that allow young children to do farm work. Workers on large farms would see the 40-hour threshold by 2027; those on farms with 25 or fewer employees would wait until 2030.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The nation's roughly two million farmworkers

how_it_helps.text: Requires agricultural employers to pay time-and-a-half after 55 hours a week beginning January 1, 2024, with the threshold stepping down to 50, 45, and then 40 hours by 2027 — the same standard other hourly workers have had for decades.
Repeals the special farmworker overtime rule (Section 7(m)) that let farms avoid overtime pay until an employee had worked 60 hours in a week or 10 hours in a day.
Strikes the minimum wage and overtime exemptions for range livestock workers and hand-harvest workers, and narrows the family exemption so only the employer's immediate family members are exempt.

Removes the child labor carve-outs for agriculture (the Section 13(h)-(j) exemptions and the exemption for child hand-harvest workers), ending the practice of children as young as 12 working long hours on farms outside school hours.
Phases in more slowly for small farms: employers with 25 or fewer employees get a three-year head start, with the 40-hour overtime threshold arriving in 2030.

analysis.who_pays: Farm employers — growers of fruit, vegetables, dairy, and livestock, and the farm labor contractors who supply crews — would bear higher labor costs, since farm work regularly involves long seasonal hours. Some of that cost would likely reach consumers through food prices, and some workers might see their scheduled hours reduced to avoid overtime.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm employers, farm labor contractors, and food prices

drawbacks.text: Labor is one of the largest costs in farming, and the bill's own structure concedes the strain: it gives farms with 25 or fewer employees a three-year delay and phases the 40-hour threshold in over four years, acknowledging that immediate compliance could be difficult for growers.

For a worker putting in 55 hours or more a week, the bill changes nothing until 2024 at the earliest — and workers on small farms would not reach the 40-hour overtime threshold until 2030, so the practical benefit is years away even if enacted.

Growers would have honest options other than paying overtime: cutting scheduled hours, accelerating mechanization, or passing costs into food prices, so the gains to individual workers are not guaranteed to equal the added cost to the industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and overdue: no other group of full-time hourly workers is legally denied overtime at 40 hours, and the exemptions being repealed date to an era of open discrimination against agricultural labor. The cost is also real, since seasonal farm work concentrates long hours in short windows and growers operate on thin margins. The bill tries to manage that with a long phase-in and a small-farm delay, which makes compliance easier but also delays the benefit to workers — a worker needing relief in 2024 gets only a 55-hour overtime threshold that year. On balance it is a straightforward pro-worker bill whose main design flaw is how slowly it delivers the goods.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and never heard from again — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Alex Padilla introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act on July 12, 2023, with 12 other original cosponsors, all Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, the standard first step; no committee action followed.

The bill finished with 14 cosponsors (13 Democrats, 1 Independent) and no Republican support, and its last recorded action is the July 2023 referral — it sat in committee until the 118th Congress expired on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers came out ahead: with the bill dead, farms keep paying overtime only after 60 hours (or not at all for many workers) and keep the exemptions covering hand-harvest crews and child labor. Farmworkers gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agricultural employers who kept the exemptions

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so the chamber's actual split is unknown; all 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (fruit, vegetable, dairy, and livestock growers)
industries.note: The bill removes the industry's decades-old carve-outs from overtime, minimum wage, and child labor law, raising labor costs during peak harvest weeks. Growers profit from the current system by paying straight time past 40 hours and, in the hand-harvest exemptions, by employing children — which is why their interest runs against the workers the bill covers.

Contractors supplying hand-harvest and range crews rely on the piece-rate and young-worker exemptions this bill repeals, and would face the same overtime and minimum wage rules as other employers of hourly labor.

Some share of higher farm labor costs would likely pass into produce and dairy prices, but the amounts would be small relative to total food spending, and the public also benefits when the workers producing its food are paid by the same rules as everyone else.
